e.t: Belteshazzar is a personal name, referring to the Babylonian name used for Daniel. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears eight times, all in Daniel, from Daniel 2:26 through Daniel 5:12. The name is used when Daniel is addressed or identified in his role within the Babylonian court. Because the word functions as a name rather than a description or action, its central meaning is the person it designates: Belteshazzar. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “seek”: it expresses an intentional action. In its only occurrence in the Hebrew Old Testament, it functions as a verb, describing something a person does rather than naming a person, place, or thing. The word presents seeking as deliberate activity. Its precise force in Ezekiel 34:12 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which provide the immediate context.

Gob is a Hebrew proper name, rendered “Gob.” It functions as a place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 2 Samuel 21:18–19. Since the available wording identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its precise significance in those passages depends on the broader context. The name itself remains consistently rendered “Gob.”

Geder is a proper name preserved in English as “Geder,” rather than translated as a descriptive word. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Joshua 12:13. Because the available record identifies the word through this name rendering but provides no explicit definition or surrounding verse text, its normal role can be stated most safely: it functions as a named designation, not as a general description or action. Its precise significance in Joshua 12:13 depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to the “neck,” naming the part of the body between the head and shoulders. It functions as a noun and appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Proverbs. Its occurrences are found in Proverbs 1:9, 3:3, 3:22, and 6:21. The surrounding wording determines what is being said about the neck in each passage, but the word itself carries this straightforward bodily meaning.

This Hebrew word refers to “Lucifer,” the English rendering used for it. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 14:12. Thus, its scriptural use is limited to that single occurrence rather than being a broadly repeated biblical term. The word functions as a distinctive designation in that passage; understanding its full force requires the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here. Its identity is preserved as a Hebrew word and should not be merged with similarly rendered words from another biblical language.

Its references include Genesis 4:8, Exodus 21:14, and Judges 9:56, but the exact force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

The word occurs 62 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing repeated use for such observances rather than a single isolated event. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the feast being discussed.

This Hebrew word means “refrain.” It is a verb, so it names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Bible corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Isaiah 48:9. That single occurrence identifies its normal lexical sense, while the surrounding verse determines how the action is being expressed in that passage. Its precise significance as a name is not established by the available lexical information, so it is best understood simply as the proper name Hamul.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “trust”—to place confidence in someone for safety, protection, or help. In the Old Testament, it commonly describes relying on God rather than merely acknowledging that he exists. Its use can express a person taking refuge in the LORD, and it may also describe God as the secure refuge his people depend on. The word occurs 37 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Psalms, where trusting God is repeatedly presented as the proper response to danger, uncertainty, or need.

e.t: This word means “Ahohite”. It is an identifying term used with people’s names, marking a person as an Ahohite. The word identifies people rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Hezro.” It identifies a man listed among David’s mighty men. The name appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in two verses: twice in 2 Samuel 23:35 and once in 1 Chronicles 11:37. Because it functions as a name rather than a common noun or verb, its ordinary meaning is identification of this person, not a description of an action or quality.

Its precise function is to characterize something as remaining present or recurring over time; the surrounding verse identifies what is continual in each passage.

This Hebrew word is the name “Judah.” It functions as a proper name, identifying Judah in Old Testament passages. Within this Hebrew corpus, it occurs seven times, appearing in Ezra and Daniel. The wording consistently points to Judah rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise role in any individual sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary lexical meaning is the name Judah.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of becoming “longer.” It functions as the predicate of a sentence, stating what happens or is true of the subject. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 20:5, so its ordinary lexical range is represented by a single recorded use. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning points to an increase in length. In genealogical passages, it functions as the action connecting a parent with a child. The word occurs 500 times in the Old Testament, showing that it is a regular term for describing birth throughout Israel’s Scriptures. Its broader force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word means “sat,” functioning as a verb that describes a person’s sitting. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, both within 2 Samuel 23:8, so its recorded use is concentrated in one passage rather than spread across many books or situations. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic lexical idea is the action or state of sitting.

Jethlah is a Hebrew proper name, preserved as “Jethlah” in the King James Version rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 19:42. e.t: This word is the personal name Esther, referring to the Jewish woman who became queen in the Persian court. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 55 times, all in the book of Esther, from Esther 2:7 through Esther 9:32. The surrounding account presents the name in commands, speeches, and actions involving Esther, including the king’s giving and the people’s response. Its ordinary meaning is therefore the name “Esther,” identifying the central woman in that biblical book.

This Hebrew verb means “awake.” It describes being conscious rather than asleep and can express becoming awake or calling attention to wakefulness.
